newsitem.title: USA: Meridian to merge with Cairn in $234 million stock deal.
newsitem.headline: Meridian to merge with Cairn in $234 million stock deal.

text.p: Meridian Resource Corp. agreed to acquire Cairn Energy USA Inc. in a $234 million stock deal that combines two of the fastest-growing oil and natural gas producers operating along the Gulf of Mexico, the companies said on Monday.

Shareholders will receive 1.08 Meridian shares for each Cairn share in a deal expected to close by early in the fourth quarter that will nearly double Meridian's market capitalisation to $425 million, Meridian Chairman Joseph Reeves said.

"It's a natural extension for each of us to expand our exploration base and to expand our production base. This is not just a merger of producing properties in the same region. This is a merger of two philosophies of growth-minded companies," Reeves said on a conference call with analysts.

Both companies have been actively using three-dimensional seismic surveys to locate oil and gas reserves, and the combined company will have a portfolio of more than 200 drilling prospects located on 150,000 acres in coastal Texas and Louisiana and the offshore Gulf of Mexico.
Houston-based Meridian operates primarily in the onshore and coastal areas of Louisiana and Texas.
Cairn, based in Dallas, has offshore operations on the outer continental shelf of the Gulf of Mexico. It was formerly a subsidiary of Cairn Energy Plc, a British oil exploration company.

The combined company would have proven reserves of 164 billion cubic feet equivalent at the end of 1996 generating an estimated $395 million in pretax cash flow. Meridian will maintain capital spending levels at about $90 million to $100 million in 1998 after the merger, unchanged from the combined spending of the two companies this year, Reeves said.

Cairn's stock fell $1.69 to $11.75 in early afternoon Nasdaq trading on concerns the deal would slow the combined growth rates of the two companies and dampen earnings after accounting for costs of the merger.

"Let me be devil's advocate for a minute. What I see is you have two very successful companies that were operating in two separate arenas, very successfully in each case. I don't understand why putting the two together is better," Houston analyst Chuck Strain said.
Reeves defended the deal as an opportunity to combine two independents with similar philosophies of aggressive growth through the drill bit.

"You know, God didn't quit putting hydrocarbons at the shoreline of Louisiana or Texas. And the geology, while it may be different in some respects offshore than onshore, the geophysics is not that much different," Reeves said.
Meridian shares fell $1 to $11.31 on the New York Stock Exchange.
